title: Numbers With Exactly Four Divisors
statement:
You get an array of positive integers nums. Some of them have exactly four positive divisors, counting 1 and the number itself.

For every such number, add up its four divisors. Return the grand total over the whole array. Numbers with any other divisor count add nothing. A value that appears several times is counted each time. Return 0 if no number qualifies.

examples.why: 21 has divisors 1, 3, 7, 21, summing to 32. 4 has three divisors (1, 2, 4) and 7 has two, so they add nothing.
8 has divisors 1, 2, 4, 8 (sum 15) and appears twice. 30 has eight divisors, so it adds nothing.
16 is a power of a single prime like 8, but it has five divisors: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

hints: Divisors come in pairs: if d divides x, so does x / d. How far do you need to search to find them all?
Trial division up to √x finds every pair. Stop early as soon as you have more than four divisors.
Be careful with perfect squares: when d · d = x, the pair is one divisor, not two. That is exactly why 4, 9 and 16 do not qualify.

explain.intuition:
You do not have to try every number up to x. Divisors pair up: d and x / d, with one of them always at most √x. So trying d from 1 to √x finds every divisor, about 316 checks for the largest inputs instead of 100 000.

Collect the divisors as you go and give up as soon as there are more than four. Perfect squares are the subtle case: d = √x is its own partner, so it adds one divisor, not two. Numbers with exactly four divisors turn out to be either p · q for two different primes or p³, which is why 8 counts but 16 does not.
steps: For d from 1 while d · d ≤ x: if d divides x, add d; and if x / d ≠ d, add x / d as well.
If count is exactly 4, add sum to the answer.
pitfalls: Counting the square root twice for a perfect square, which makes 4, 9 or 49 look like they have four divisors.
Testing only "is it a product of two primes" and forgetting cubes like 8 and 27.
Trying every d up to x: 10 000 numbers × 100 000 checks is far too slow.

solutions.title: Try every possible divisor
solutions.idea: Test every d from 1 to x and count the ones that divide x.

solutions.title: Divisor pairs up to the square root
solutions.idea: Each divisor d ≤ √x brings its partner x / d. Stop as soon as more than four are found.

followups: There are a million queries over values up to 10⁶. How would a smallest-prime-factor sieve answer each in O(log x)?
Return the sum for numbers with exactly k divisors. What does the prime factorisation tell you about the divisor count?
